title: SQL in depth: joins, GROUP BY, subqueries
summary: Combine tables with joins, summarise rows with GROUP BY, and answer harder questions using nested subqueries.
objectives: Combine rows from two tables with INNER JOIN using a key
Keep unmatched rows with LEFT JOIN and spot the NULLs
Summarise rows into groups with GROUP BY and aggregate functions
Filter groups with HAVING and understand how it differs from WHERE
Answer harder questions by nesting a subquery inside a query
Read a query in the order the database actually runs it

quiz.q: Which join keeps every row from the left table even when there is no match on the right?
quiz.why: LEFT JOIN returns all left-table rows; unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL.

quiz.q: You want to filter on the result of COUNT(*) per group. Which clause do you use?
quiz.why: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation.

options: Collapses rows that share a value into one row per group
quiz.why: GROUP BY buckets rows by the column(s) you name, so aggregates like SUM and COUNT run per bucket.

quiz.q: In SQL, what is a subquery?
quiz.answer: A query nested inside another query, whose result feeds the outer query.
quiz.why: Subqueries can sit in WHERE, FROM, or SELECT and let you compute a value to compare or join against.

quiz.q: Write the aggregate function that counts the number of rows in each group.
quiz.why: COUNT(*) counts all rows per group; COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values in that column.

quiz.q: WHERE and HAVING run at different times. Which runs first?
options: They run at the same time
quiz.why: WHERE filters rows before grouping; only then does GROUP BY form groups and HAVING filter them.

body_markdown:
## Why go deeper than SELECT?

A single table rarely holds the whole story. Customers live in one table, their orders in another. To answer real questions — *how much did each customer spend?* — you must **combine** tables and **summarise** rows. That is what joins, GROUP BY, and subqueries give you.

As a maths graduate, think of a table as a relation: a set of tuples. A **join** is like an intersection over a shared key, and **GROUP BY** is partitioning a set into equivalence classes, then applying a function to each class.

## Joins: combining tables on a key

A join matches rows from two tables using a shared column, usually an id. An **INNER JOIN** keeps only rows that match in both tables. A **LEFT JOIN** keeps every row from the left table and fills missing right-side values with `NULL`.

```sql
-- Every order with its customer's name
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN customers AS c
  ON o.customer_id = c.id;

-- Customers WITH or WITHOUT orders
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

Use table **aliases** (`o`, `c`) to keep queries short, and always say which table a column comes from when names could clash.

## GROUP BY and aggregates

**GROUP BY** collapses rows that share a value into one row per group. You then apply an **aggregate function** — `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` — to each group.

```sql
-- Total and average spend per customer
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*)    AS num_orders,
       SUM(amount) AS total_spent,
       AVG(amount) AS avg_order
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > 100
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
```

Every column in `SELECT` must either be inside an aggregate or listed in `GROUP BY`.

## WHERE vs HAVING

This trips up everyone. **WHERE** filters individual rows *before* grouping. **HAVING** filters whole groups *after* aggregation. If you need `COUNT(*) > 3`, that condition belongs in `HAVING`, because the count does not exist until groups are formed.

## Subqueries: a query inside a query

A **subquery** is a SELECT nested inside another statement. Its result feeds the outer query. Use one to compare against a computed value, or to build a temporary table to join against.

```sql
-- Customers who spent more than the average customer
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
  HAVING SUM(amount) > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders)
);
```

## How SQL actually runs

SQL is not read top to bottom. The engine runs roughly: `FROM` and joins, then `WHERE`, then `GROUP BY`, then `HAVING`, then `SELECT`, then `ORDER BY`, then `LIMIT`. Knowing this order explains why you cannot use a `SELECT` alias in `WHERE`, but can in `ORDER BY`.

## Your task

Take a two-table dataset (orders and customers, or any pair you have). Write one query with a `LEFT JOIN`, one with `GROUP BY` plus `HAVING`, and one that uses a subquery. Explain in a sentence what each answers.

slides.narration: Welcome back to Month Two. You already know how to pull rows from a single table with S Q L. In this lesson we go deeper. You'll learn to combine tables with joins, to summarise many rows into group totals with GROUP BY, and to answer harder questions by nesting one query inside another with subqueries. These three ideas unlock almost every real data question.

slides.title: Why go deeper?
bullets: One table rarely holds the whole story.
Customers in one table, orders in another.
Joins combine, GROUP BY summarises.
Maths view: relations, keys, partitions.
slides.narration: Why isn't a simple SELECT enough? Because real data is spread across tables. Customers sit in one table, their orders in another. To ask how much each customer spent, you must combine the two and then summarise. As a maths graduate, think of a table as a relation, a join as matching on a shared key, and GROUP BY as partitioning a set into classes.

slides.title: INNER JOIN
bullets: Match rows on a shared key.
Keeps only rows that match in both.
Use aliases to keep it short.
Say which table each column is from.
slides.code:
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN customers AS c
  ON o.customer_id = c.id;
slides.narration: Let's start with the inner join. It matches rows from two tables using a shared column, here the customer id. An inner join keeps only the rows that have a match in both tables. Notice the aliases, o for orders and c for customers. They keep the query short, and they let us say exactly which table each column comes from.

slides.title: LEFT JOIN and NULLs
bullets: Keeps every row from the left table.
Unmatched right-side columns become NULL.
Great for finding what's missing.
Customers with zero orders still appear.
slides.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id;
slides.narration: Sometimes you want rows even when there's no match. A left join keeps every row from the left table, and where the right table has nothing, it fills the columns with NULL. This is perfect for finding gaps. If a customer has placed no orders, an inner join would hide them, but a left join shows them with a NULL order id.

slides.title: GROUP BY
bullets: Collapses rows sharing a value into one.
One output row per group.
Apply aggregates to each group.
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
slides.code:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*)    AS num_orders,
       SUM(amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
slides.narration: Now to summarising. GROUP BY collapses all rows that share a value into a single output row per group. Then you apply an aggregate function to each group. Here we group orders by customer id, and for each customer we count their orders and sum their spend. The big rule: every column you select must be inside an aggregate or listed in the GROUP BY.

slides.title: WHERE vs HAVING
bullets: WHERE filters rows before grouping.
HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
Need COUNT(*) > 3? Use HAVING.
The count doesn't exist until grouping.
slides.code:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
WHERE amount > 0
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > 100;
slides.narration: Here's the distinction that trips up almost everyone. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens. HAVING filters whole groups after the aggregates are computed. So if you want only customers whose total spend is over a hundred, that goes in HAVING, because the sum simply doesn't exist until the groups are formed.

slides.title: Subqueries
bullets: A query nested inside another query.
Its result feeds the outer query.
Lives in WHERE, FROM, or SELECT.
Compute a value, then compare to it.
slides.code:
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
);
slides.narration: A subquery is simply a query nested inside another query. The inner query runs first and its result feeds the outer one. Here the inner query produces a list of customer ids that have orders, and the outer query returns the names of those customers. Subqueries can live in the WHERE clause, in FROM as a temporary table, or even in SELECT.

slides.title: Subquery: above average
bullets: Compare a group against the whole table.
Inner query computes the average.
Outer query keeps the big spenders.
One question, two levels of logic.
slides.code:
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) >
  (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders);
slides.narration: Here's a more powerful example. We want customers who spend more than the average order. The inner subquery computes one number, the average amount across all orders. The outer query groups by customer and keeps only those whose total beats that average. Notice how a subquery lets you compare a group against a value drawn from the whole table.

slides.title: How SQL really runs
bullets: FROM and joins, then WHERE.
Then GROUP BY, then HAVING.
Then SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
Explains why aliases work where they do.
slides.code:
-- logical order:
-- FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY
-- -> HAVING -> SELECT
-- -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT
slides.narration: One last idea that makes everything click. S Q L is not read top to bottom. The engine runs FROM and the joins first, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, and finally LIMIT. This order explains why you can't use a SELECT alias inside WHERE, but you can inside ORDER BY, because ORDER BY runs after SELECT.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Selecting a column not in GROUP BY.
Putting an aggregate filter in WHERE.
Forgetting LEFT JOIN can produce NULLs.
Ambiguous columns without a table alias.
slides.narration: Let's flag the mistakes that catch almost everyone. One: selecting a column that's neither aggregated nor in the GROUP BY. Two: trying to filter on a COUNT or SUM inside WHERE instead of HAVING. Three: forgetting that a left join introduces NULLs you must handle. And four: leaving a column ambiguous when both tables share the name. Always prefix with the table alias.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Joins combine tables on a key.
GROUP BY plus aggregates summarise groups.
HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters rows.
Subqueries nest one query inside another.
Task: write a join, a GROUP BY, a subquery.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Joins combine tables on a shared key, with inner keeping matches and left keeping every left row. GROUP BY plus aggregates summarise rows into group totals. WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after. And subqueries nest one query inside another to answer harder questions. Your task: on a two table dataset, write one left join, one GROUP BY with HAVING, and one subquery, and say what each answers. See you next lesson.
